lessons.sub: Why security people use Python, and how to store a value.
learn: Why Python
Python is the most common scripting language in security. Analysts use it to parse logs, call APIs, automate checks and glue tools together. Kali already has Python 3 installed.
Two ways to run it
Type `python3` to open the interactive prompt and try lines one at a time. Or save code in a file ending in .py and run `python3 hello.py`. Leave the prompt with `exit()`.
print and comments
`print()` shows output. Anything after `#` is a comment that Python ignores. Use comments to explain why, not what.

# Say hello to the SOC
print("Hello, SOC")
print(2 + 3)
Variables
A variable is a name for a value. You create one by assigning to it with `=`. Pick names that say what the value is, like `target_ip`, not `x`.

target_ip = "10.10.10.20"
port = 445
print(target_ip, port)
The core types
`str` is text, `int` is a whole number, `float` has a decimal point and `bool` is True or False. `type()` tells you which one you have.

play.p: Change the message and the port, then tap Run.
play.code:
host = "10.10.10.20"
port = 445
print("Checking", host, "on port", port)

real: On the job
A SOC analyst gets 2,000 alerts exported to a file. Reading them by hand takes a day. A 15-line script sorts and counts them in a second. That's why so many security job ads mention Python.
myth: You have to be a programmer to use Python in security.
Most security scripts are short: read something, filter it, count it, print it. You'll write useful ones by the end of this track.

tryit.p: Create a file, run it, then change the message and run it again.
tryit.code:
echo 'print("Hello from Kali")' > hello.py
python3 hello.py

quiz.w: The second line is a comment, so only `print(2 + 3)` runs.
The decimal point makes it a float, even though the value is a whole number.

quiz.q: How do you run a script saved as scan.py?
quiz.w: Give the file to the python3 interpreter.

challenge.p: Store the name of your lab target in a variable called `target`, then print `Target: win10`.
challenge.hint: Put the text between the quotes on the first line.
challenge.solution:
target = "win10"
print("Target:", target)

recap: Python is the security team's glue language.
Run it with `python3` or `python3 file.py`.
`print()` shows output; `#` starts a comment.
Assign with `=` and use descriptive names.

lessons.sub: Text, numbers, and building readable output.
learn: Text isn't a number
Anything you read from a file, a log or user input arrives as text. "22" + "1" joins text into "221"; it doesn't add. Convert with `int()` before doing maths.
Converting
`int("22")` turns text into a number and `str(22)` turns a number into text. Converting text that isn't a number, like `int("ssh")`, raises a ValueError.
f-strings
Put an f before the quotes and you can drop variables straight into text with braces. They're the clearest way to build output and messages.

ip = "10.10.10.20"
open_ports = 3
print(f"{ip} has {open_ports} open ports")

play.p: Edit the values and run it again. Try putting a calculation inside the curly brackets.
play.code:
ip = "10.10.10.20"
open_ports = 3
print(f"{ip} has {open_ports} open ports")
print(f"Next port: {22 + 1}")

real: On the job

A firewall export lists ports as text. A script that checks `"80" > "443"` says True, because text compares character by character and 8 beats 4. As numbers, 80 > 443 is False. Converting to int first fixes it.
myth: Python works out what you meant, so types don't matter.
Python won't guess. Mixing text and numbers either raises an error or quietly does the wrong thing.

tryit.p: Type each line into the Python prompt and predict the result before you press Enter.

quiz.w: Both values are text, so `+` joins them.
`int()` converts the text to a number first, so this is real addition.
The f prefix fills in the braces with the variable's value.

challenge.p: The log gives the port as text. Add 1 to it as a number and print `next port: 23` using an f-string.
challenge.hint: Convert with `int(port)` inside the curly brackets.
challenge.solution:
port = "22"
print(f"next port: {int(port) + 1}")

recap: Input from files and logs is text.
Convert with `int()` and `str()` before mixing.
f-strings put values inside `{}`.
You can do maths inside the brackets.

lessons.sub: Make decisions in code.
learn: if, elif, else
An if runs its block only when the condition is true. elif checks the next condition and else catches everything left. Only the first matching branch runs.
Comparisons
`==` means equal and `!=` means not equal. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare numbers. Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`. A single `=` assigns; it never compares.
Indentation is syntax
Python groups code by indentation, not braces. Lines inside an if or a loop are indented, usually by four spaces. What Python requires is consistency; getting it wrong is an error, not a style issue.

play.p: Change `fails` to 2, 6 and 12 and see which branch runs.

real: On the job
Every alert rule is an if statement underneath: if failed logins from one IP go over a threshold in five minutes, raise an alert. Tuning the threshold is a daily SOC job.
myth: `=` and `==` mean the same thing.
`=` stores a value; `==` compares two values. Writing `if fails = 5:` is a syntax error in Python.

quiz.w: 3 isn't over 10 or over 5, so neither the if nor the elif runs, and the else branch prints ok.

quiz.q: What happens when you run this?
quiz.w: The body of an if must be indented. Python refuses to run the file.
Both checks are written with `==`, and `role` equals "admin", so the first branch runs.

challenge.p: Print `high` if `cvss` is 7.0 or more, otherwise print `low`.
challenge.hint: Use `if cvss >= 7.0:` with an `else:`. Indent each print by four spaces.

recap: if, elif and else choose one branch.
`==` compares; `=` assigns.
Indentation decides what's inside the if.
Rules and alerts are conditions underneath.

lessons.sub: Keep many values in order.
learn: Lists
A list holds items in order, in square brackets. Get an item by its index, starting at 0. `len()` gives the number of items and `.append()` adds one to the end.

ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(ports[0], len(ports))
Changing a list
`.append(x)` adds to the end and `.remove(x)` takes the first match out. `len(ports)` tells you how many items there are.

ports = [22, 80]
ports.append(443)
ports.remove(80)
print(ports, len(ports))
Slicing
`ports[0:2]` gives the first two items. The start is included and the end isn't, just like `range`. `ports[-1]` is the last item.

ports = [21, 22, 80, 443]
print(ports[0:2], ports[-1])

play.p: Add another port to the list, then print the last one.
play.code:
ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(ports)
print("last:", ports[-1])

real: On the job
An asset list of 400 hosts is a list. Sorting it, removing decommissioned hosts and comparing it with what the scanner saw is where shadow IT gets found.
myth: The first item in a list is item 1.
Python counts from 0, so `ports[0]` is the first item and `ports[1]` is the second.

quiz.w: Index 1 is the second item, because counting starts at 0.
`.remove(80)` takes 80 out, leaving 22 and 443.
The slice starts at index 0 and stops before index 2.

challenge.p: Add 3389 to the list, then print how many ports there are.
challenge.hint: Use `.append(3389)` then `print(len(ports))`.
challenge.solution:
ports = [22, 80, 443]
ports.append(3389)
print(len(ports))

recap: Lists hold ordered items.
Indexes start at 0, and -1 is the last item.
`.append()` adds; `.remove()` takes out.
Slices include the start, not the end.

lessons.sub: Do the same thing to every item.
learn: for loops
A for loop runs its indented block once for each item. This is how you check every host, every port or every log line.

for port in [22, 80, 443]:
    print("checking", port)
range
`range(1, 5)` produces 1, 2, 3 and 4. The end number is not included. It's handy for port ranges and counting.
Filtering as you go
Combine a loop and an if to keep only what matters. Build a new list of matches, then work with that.

play.p: Change the list and the condition, then run it.

real: On the job
A vulnerability scanner returns 500 findings. A loop that keeps only the critical ones on internet-facing hosts gives you a short list to fix first.
myth: `range(1, 5)` includes 5.
The stop value is excluded, so `range(1, 5)` gives 1 to 4. For ports 1 to 1024, write `range(1, 1025)`.

tryit.p: Loop over your lab addresses and print a line for each. Then change it to skip the Kali address.

quiz.w: The start is included and the stop is not.

quiz.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 4, 5]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
quiz.w: The loop adds each number to the running total: 3, then 7, then 12.

quiz.code:
count = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    count += 1
print(count)
quiz.w: The loop runs for 1, 2 and 3, adding 1 to `count` each time.

challenge.p: Loop over the list and print only the ports below 1024, one per line.
challenge.hint: Use `for p in ports:` and inside it `if p < 1024:`.

recap: for loops run once per item.
`range(a, b)` stops before b.
A loop plus an if filters a list.
`count += 1` adds one each time round.

lessons.sub: Look things up by name.
learn: Dictionaries
A dictionary maps keys to values, in curly braces. Look a value up by its key, the way DNS looks up an address by name.

services = {22: "ssh", 80: "http", 443: "https"}
print(services[443])
Safe lookups
Looking up a missing key with square brackets raises a KeyError. `.get(key, default)` returns the default instead, which is safer with messy data.
Counting by hand
To count things, add 1 to a dictionary value each time you see a key. Start missing keys at 0 with `.get()`.

play.p: Add another service, then look one up that isn't there.

real: On the job
Parsed JSON from any security API arrives as dictionaries. Knowing how to reach `alert["src"]["ip"]` safely is half of every automation script.
myth: Dictionaries are only for advanced code.
They're one of the most useful beginner tools: look-up tables, counts and parsed JSON are all dictionaries.

quiz.w: 443 isn't a key, so `.get()` returns the default you gave it.

o: The first time an IP appears it isn't a key yet
quiz.w: Square brackets on a missing key raise a KeyError. `.get` starts new keys at 0.
`.get` returns the default you give it when the key is missing.

challenge.p: Count how many times each user appears and print the dictionary.
challenge.hint: Loop over `users` and use `counts[u] = counts.get(u, 0) + 1`.

recap: Dictionaries map keys to values.
`.get(key, default)` avoids KeyErrors.
Count with `.get(k, 0) + 1`.
API data usually arrives as dictionaries.

lessons.sub: Package code you'll reuse.
learn: Functions
`def` defines a function: a named block you can call again and again. Parameters go in the brackets, and `return` sends a result back.
Why functions matter
Functions stop you copying code around. Fix a bug once and every caller gets the fix. They also make scripts easier to test and read.
Parameters and defaults
A parameter can have a default: `def check(port, timeout=1):`. Callers can leave it out or pass their own value.

def check(port, timeout=1):
    return f"port {port}, timeout {timeout}"

print(check(22))
print(check(22, 5))

play.p: Change the threshold, or call the function with different numbers.
play.code:
def suspicious(fails, threshold=5):
    return fails > threshold

print(suspicious(3))
print(suspicious(8))
print(suspicious(8, threshold=10))

real: On the job
Detection rules are functions in disguise: given an event, return True if it's suspicious. Writing small functions like `is_off_hours(timestamp)` is exactly how SIEM and SOAR logic is built.
myth: A function that prints a result returns it too.
print shows a value on screen; return hands it back to the caller. A function without return gives back None.

tryit.p: Write a function that flags a login as suspicious after more than five failures, then test it with a few values.

quiz.w: The function multiplies its two arguments and returns 12.

quiz.code:
def check(port):
    print("checked", port)

result = check(22)
print(result)
quiz.w: The function prints but never returns, so `result` is None.
`timeout` wasn't passed, so it uses its default of 1.

challenge.p: Write a function `is_admin_port(port)` that returns True for 22, 3389 and 5985, then print `is_admin_port(3389)`.
challenge.hint: Replace `pass` with `return port in (22, 3389, 5985)`.

recap: `def` packages code; `return` hands back a result.
A function without return gives back None.
Defaults make parameters optional.
Small functions make detection logic readable.

lessons.sub: Clean, split and search text.
learn: String methods
Strings come with built-in methods. `.lower()` and `.upper()` change case, `.strip()` removes spaces and newlines from the ends, and `.replace()` swaps text.

user = "  Admin \n"
print(user.strip().lower())
Split into parts
`.split()` breaks a string into a list of words. With an argument it splits on that character instead. It's the quickest way to pull fields out of a log line.

line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5"
parts = line.split()
print(parts[-1])
Searching
`in` checks whether text appears anywhere in a string. `.startswith()` and `.endswith()` check the ends. All of them are case-sensitive.

play.p: Change the log line and see what each method gives you.
play.code:
line = "  Failed password for ROOT from 10.0.0.5  "
clean = line.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean.split()[-1])
print(clean.startswith("failed"))

real: On the job
Phishing triage often starts with string checks: does the sender's domain end with your company's domain, or with a look-alike? A couple of `.endswith()` and `.lower()` calls handle that.
myth: `in` and `==` do the same thing.
`==` needs an exact match. `in` finds text anywhere, so "admin" in "sysadmin" is True. That difference causes real filtering bugs.

tryit.h: Pull fields from a log line
tryit.p: Split a real-looking SSH log line and print the user and IP address.
tryit.code:
line = "Failed password for invalid user test from 10.10.10.10 port 51234 ssh2"
parts = line.split()
print("user:", parts[5])
print("ip:", parts[7])

quiz.w: Counting starts at 0: Failed is 0, password is 1, for is 2.
`in` matches anywhere inside the string, which is easy to forget when filtering usernames.
`.endswith` checks the end of the text exactly.

challenge.p: Print just the username from this log line, in lower case: `root`.
challenge.hint: `.split()` gives a list of words. The username is at index 3. Then use `.lower()`.
challenge.solution:
line = "Failed password for ROOT from 10.0.0.5"
print(line.split()[3].lower())

recap: `.strip()`, `.lower()` and `.split()` do most clean-up.
`in` matches anywhere; `==` needs an exact match.
`.startswith()` and `.endswith()` check the edges.
Split, then pick the part you need.

lessons.t: Parse a log: failed SSH logins
lessons.sub: Count failures in a real-looking auth log.
learn: Open with with
`with open(path) as f:` opens a file and closes it automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens. Use it every time.
Line by line
Looping over a file gives one line at a time, so even a huge log fits in memory. Each line ends with a newline, which `.strip()` removes.
Messy logs
Real logs contain odd characters. `open(path, errors="replace")` swaps unreadable bytes for a placeholder instead of crashing halfway through.
Practise on text first
Here a sample log is stored in a variable, and `.splitlines()` turns it into lines. On Kali you'd loop over an open file instead; the loop body stays the same.

play.p: The sample log is in `LOG`. Run it, then change what it counts, for example `Accepted`.
play.code:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
count = 0
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    if "Failed password" in line:
        count += 1
print(count, "failed logins")

real: On the job

An incident responder receives a 2 GB web server log. Opening it in Notepad hangs the laptop. A Python loop reads it line by line, keeps only requests from the suspect IP and writes them to a small file.
myth: You must load the whole file before searching it.
Looping over the file object reads one line at a time. That's faster to start and works on files bigger than your RAM.

tryit.p: SSH isn't running on Kali by default. Start it, fail a login, export the log, then count the failures with Python.
tryit.code:
sudo systemctl start ssh
ssh nobody@localhost    # type yes, a wrong password, then Ctrl+C
sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log
python3 -c '
count = 0
with open("ssh.log", errors="replace") as f:
    for line in f:
        if "Failed password" in line:
            count += 1
print(count, "failed logins")
'
sudo systemctl stop ssh

quiz.q: What does `with open(...) as f:` give you that plain `open()` doesn't?
o: The file closes automatically when the block ends
quiz.w: The with block guarantees the file is closed, even if an error interrupts it.

quiz.q: Why loop over a log file line by line instead of reading it all at once?
o: It handles files bigger than memory
quiz.w: Only one line is held at a time, so file size stops mattering.

quiz.code:
log = "Failed a\nAccepted b\nFailed c"
print(sum(1 for l in log.splitlines() if "Failed" in l))
quiz.w: Two of the three lines contain "Failed".

challenge.p: Print each source IP of a failed login, one per line. The IP is the word after `from`.
challenge.start:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    if "Failed password" in line:
        parts = line.split()
challenge.hint: `parts.index("from")` gives the position of `from`, so the IP is at that position plus 1.
challenge.solution:
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    if "Failed password" in line:
        parts = line.split()
        print(parts[parts.index("from") + 1])

recap: Always open files with `with`.
Loop line by line; never load a huge log at once.
Find the field by a nearby word, not a fixed position.
`errors="replace"` survives messy logs.

lessons.sub: Remove duplicates and compare groups.
learn: What a set is
A set holds unique values with no order. `set(ips)` throws away duplicates, so `len(set(ips))` counts distinct IPs.
Comparing sets
`a - b` is what's in a but not b. `a & b` is what's in both. That's how you compare what the scanner found with your asset list.
Sorting for output
Sets have no order, so their printed order can change. Use `sorted(myset)` when you want stable, readable output.

play.p: Change the lists and see which hosts are unknown.

real: On the job
Comparing "hosts on the network" with "hosts in the asset register" is how shadow IT is found. With sets it's one line: `seen - registered`.
myth: A set keeps items in the order you added them.
It doesn't promise any order. If order matters, use a list or sort the set when you print it.

quiz.w: The set keeps one copy of each address, so there are two.
`a - b` keeps what's only in a.

quiz.q: Why print `sorted(myset)` instead of the set itself?
quiz.w: Sorting gives stable, readable output each time.

challenge.p: Print the unique failed-login IPs, sorted, as a list.
challenge.hint: `sorted(set(fails))` removes duplicates and sorts in one go.

recap: Sets keep one copy of each value.
`a - b` finds what's missing; `a & b` finds the overlap.
Sets have no order, so sort before printing.
Great for comparing asset lists.

lessons.sub: Count things in one line.
learn: Counter does it for you
`collections.Counter` counts a list in one line, and `.most_common(n)` gives the top n. It's perfect for top talkers and top failed-login sources.

from collections import Counter
fails = ["1.1.1.1", "2.2.2.2", "1.1.1.1"]
print(Counter(fails).most_common(1))
most_common
`Counter(ips).most_common(3)` gives the top three as (value, count) pairs, already sorted. Perfect for a "top attackers" report.
Counters add up
You can update a Counter as you go with `c[ip] += 1`. A missing key starts at 0, so there's no KeyError.

play.p: Change the list and the number passed to `most_common`.
play.code:
from collections import Counter
ips = ["203.0.113.7", "198.51.100.23", "203.0.113.7", "203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.4"]
for ip, n in Counter(ips).most_common(2):
    print(ip, n)

real: On the job
“Which IPs failed to log in the most last night?” is a daily SOC question. Read the log, pull out the IPs, put them in a Counter, print `most_common(10)`. Done.

tryit.p: Count how often each IP appears and print the top two.
tryit.code:
from collections import Counter
ips = ["10.10.10.20", "10.10.10.30", "10.10.10.20", "8.8.8.8", "10.10.10.20"]
for ip, n in Counter(ips).most_common(2):
    print(ip, n)

myth: You need a database to count events.
For millions of lines, maybe. For a day's auth log, a Counter in memory is instant.

quiz.w: `most_common` returns a list of (item, count) pairs, highest first.

quiz.code:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter()
c["root"] += 1
print(c["root"])
quiz.w: Missing keys start at 0 in a Counter, so adding 1 gives 1.
`most_common(1)` returns a list holding the top pair; `[0]` takes that pair out.

challenge.p: Print the single most-targeted username and its count, like `root 3`.
challenge.hint: `Counter(users).most_common(1)[0]` gives a (name, count) pair.
challenge.solution:
from collections import Counter
users = ["root", "admin", "root", "test", "root", "admin"]
name, n = Counter(users).most_common(1)[0]
print(name, n)

recap: Counter counts a list in one line.
`most_common(n)` gives the top n.
Missing keys start at 0.
Use it for top-attacker reports.

lessons.sub: Find patterns, not just fixed text.
learn: What regex is
A regular expression is a pattern that matches text. Python's `re` module uses it to find IP addresses, usernames or error codes inside messy lines. Write patterns as raw strings, like `r"..."`.
Building blocks
`\d` matches a digit and `\S` any non-whitespace character. `+` means one or more. `.` matches any character, so escape it as `\.` when you mean a real dot.
Capture groups
Brackets capture part of a match. `re.search` returns a match object, and `.group(1)` gives you what the first brackets captured.

import re
line = "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22"
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)
if m:
    print(m.group(1))
findall
`re.findall` returns every match in the text as a list. It's the quickest way to pull all the IP addresses or numbers out of a line.

play.p: Add more addresses to the text and run it again.
play.code:
import re
text = "Blocked 10.10.10.10 and 203.0.113.7; allowed 10.10.10.20"
print(re.findall(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", text))

real: On the job
Threat intel reports list indicators like IPs and domains buried in paragraphs. A regex pulls them out in seconds so they can be blocked or searched for in your SIEM.
myth: You need to memorise regex syntax.
Nobody does. Learn the few building blocks here, then test patterns on a site like regex101 or in the Python prompt.

quiz.code:
import re
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", "Failed password for root from 10.0.0.5 port 22")
print(m.group(1))
quiz.w: The brackets capture the non-space text right after "from ".
findall returns every match as a string inside a list.

quiz.q: Why write the pattern as `r"\d+"` instead of `"\d+"`?
o: The r keeps backslashes exactly as typed
quiz.w: A raw string stops Python treating backslashes as its own escapes. Without it, `\b` (a regex word boundary) silently becomes a backspace character.

challenge.p: Use a capture group to print the IP after `from` in this line.
challenge.start:
import re
line = "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2"
challenge.hint: `re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)` then `.group(1)`.
challenge.solution:
import re
line = "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2"
m = re.search(r"from (\S+)", line)
print(m.group(1))

recap: `re.search` finds the first match; `re.findall` finds them all.
Capture groups pull out just the part you need.
Use raw strings for patterns.
Escape a real dot as `\.`.

lessons.sub: Combine checks into one useful tool.
learn: What makes a password strong
Length matters most. NIST's current guidance favours long passphrases and checking against lists of breached passwords over forced symbols and regular changes.
Checks with any()
`any(c.isdigit() for c in pw)` is True if at least one character is a digit. The same pattern works for `.isupper()` and `.islower()`.
Keep it honest
A checker can only guess. A long password that's already in a breach list is still weak, which is why real systems also check breached-password lists.

play.p: Try different passwords and watch the score change.
play.code:
pw = "Summer2024"
score = 0
if len(pw) >= 12: score += 1
if any(c.isdigit() for c in pw): score += 1
if any(c.isupper() for c in pw): score += 1
if pw.lower() not in ["password", "summer2024", "letmein"]: score += 1
print(pw, "scores", score, "out of 4")

real: On the job
Help desk staff get asked "is this a good password?" all the time. Knowing that length and breach checks matter more than symbols is a common interview question too.
myth: Adding a symbol makes any password strong.
"P@ssw0rd!" has symbols and is in every breach list. Length and uniqueness matter more.

quiz.code:
pw = "hunter9"
print(any(c.isdigit() for c in pw))
quiz.w: "9" is a digit, so `any` finds one.

o: Your old password with the year changed
quiz.w: Length and uniqueness beat complexity rules. Changing a year is easy to guess.
"abc" has no upper-case letters.

challenge.p: Write `strong(pw)` that returns True only if the password is at least 14 characters long. Print `strong("correct horse battery")`.
challenge.hint: `return len(pw) >= 14`

recap: Length matters most.
`any(... for c in pw)` checks for a type of character.
Check against breached-password lists.
A checker estimates; it can't prove strength.

lessons.sub: Fingerprint text and files.
learn: hashlib
Python's `hashlib` computes hashes like SHA-256. Hash functions work on bytes, so encode text first with `.encode()`. `.hexdigest()` gives the familiar hex string.

import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("hello".encode()).hexdigest())
Hashing a file
Read the file in binary mode and feed it to the hash in chunks, so large files don't fill memory. Compare the result with the publisher's hash to check integrity.
Passwords need more
SHA-256 is too fast for storing passwords. Use a slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt, through a library like argon2-cffi. Never write your own.

play.p: Change one letter of the text and see how much the hash changes.
play.code:
import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("hello".encode()).hexdigest())
print(hashlib.sha256("hellp".encode()).hexdigest())

real: On the job
Malware analysts share file hashes, not files. Searching a SHA-256 in a threat intel service tells you in seconds whether a suspicious attachment is already known to be malicious.

tryit.p: Hash any file and compare the result with `sha256sum` on the same file. They should match exactly.
tryit.code:
import hashlib, sys
h = hashlib.sha256()
with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as f:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
        h.update(chunk)
print(h.hexdigest())
# run: python3 hashfile.py /etc/hostname
# compare: sha256sum /etc/hostname

myth: A hash can be reversed to get the original back.
A hash is one-way. Attackers "crack" hashes by guessing inputs and hashing them, which is why slow password hashes matter.

quiz.w: SHA-256 is 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, which is 64 hex characters.

quiz.q: Which should you use to store user passwords?
quiz.w: Password hashes must be slow and salted so stolen hashes are expensive to crack.

o: hashlib works on bytes, not strings
quiz.w: `.encode()` turns text into bytes using UTF-8.

challenge.p: Print the first 8 characters of the SHA-256 hash of `abc`.
challenge.hint: Get the hex digest, then slice it with `[:8]`.
challenge.solution:
import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256("abc".encode()).hexdigest()[:8])

recap: Hash bytes: `.encode()` text first.
A tiny change gives a completely different hash.
Hash big files in chunks, in binary mode.
Passwords need Argon2 or bcrypt.

lessons.sub: Encoding you'll see in logs and phishing, and why it isn't security.
learn: Encoding isn't encryption
Base64 turns bytes into safe text for email or URLs. Anyone can reverse it with no key. Seeing Base64 in a script or config means obscured, not protected.
Encode and decode
`base64.b64encode(b"text")` encodes bytes; `b64decode` reverses it. Both work on bytes, so use `.encode()` and `.decode()` around them.

import base64
enc = base64.b64encode("whoami".encode())
print(enc)
print(base64.b64decode(enc).decode())
Where you'll see it
Attackers use base64 to hide commands, for example `powershell -EncodedCommand`. Decoding it is often the first step in triaging a suspicious command line.

play.p: Decode the string, then encode a message of your own.
play.code:
import base64
print(base64.b64decode("aGVsbG8=").decode())
print(base64.b64encode("lab only".encode()).decode())

real: On the job
An EDR alert shows `powershell -enc` followed by a long string. Decoding it (PowerShell's version is UTF-16LE base64) reveals the real command in seconds.
myth: Base64 hides secrets.
Base64 is encoding: one line of Python reverses it. Attackers use it to dodge simple text filters, not to protect anything.

o: An error, because you need a key
quiz.w: No key needed. That's why Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

quiz.q: Is base64 a way to protect a password?
quiz.w: Base64 has no key. It's encoding, not encryption.
"hi" encodes to aGk= in base64.

challenge.p: Decode this string and print the hidden command.
challenge.hint: `base64.b64decode(secret).decode()`
challenge.solution:
import base64
secret = "bmV0IHVzZXI="
print(base64.b64decode(secret).decode())

recap: Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption.
It works on bytes: encode and decode around it.
Attackers use it to hide commands.
Decoding is a normal triage step.

lessons.sub: Scripts that survive bad input.
learn: Exceptions
When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception, like FileNotFoundError or ValueError. Unhandled, it stops the script with a traceback.
try and except
Wrap risky code in try, and handle a specific exception in except. Catch the errors you expect; a bare `except:` hides real bugs.
Fail safely
If a security check can't complete, decide what happens. A function that returns True for “allowed” when it hits an error is failing open, which is OWASP 2025 A10. Default to deny.

play.p: Change the list so every value is a number, then add more bad values.

real: On the job
A scheduled script crashes at 3am because one log line is malformed, and nobody notices for a week. Handling the expected error, logging it and carrying on keeps monitoring alive.
myth: Catching every exception with a bare except is the safe choice.
It hides bugs and can even catch Ctrl+C. Catch the specific errors you expect and let real problems surface.

quiz.w: "8080" is all digits, so `int()` works, the print runs and the except block is skipped.

quiz.q: An access check hits a database error and returns True. What's wrong?
o: It fails open, so errors grant access
quiz.w: When a check can't finish, deny by default. Failing open turns an outage into a breach.
`int("x")` raises ValueError, so the except block runs.

challenge.p: Add up only the valid port numbers and print the total. Skip anything that isn't a number.
challenge.hint: Loop over values, and wrap `total += int(v)` in try/except ValueError.

recap: Exceptions stop scripts unless handled.
Catch specific errors, not everything.
Security checks should fail safe.
Skip bad lines and keep going.

lessons.t: JSON: spot "*" in an IAM policy
lessons.sub: Read security data the way APIs send it.
learn: JSON
Most security APIs, SIEM exports and cloud logs use JSON. `json.loads()` turns JSON text into Python dictionaries and lists, and `json.dumps()` turns them back into text.
Reading nested data
Parsed JSON is just dictionaries and lists inside each other. Reach into it step by step with keys and indexes.

import json
alert = json.loads('{"rule": "brute force", "src": {"ip": "203.0.113.7"}, "count": 42}')
print(alert["src"]["ip"], alert["count"])
IAM policies are JSON
An AWS IAM policy is JSON with a list of `Statement` entries. `"Action": "*"` with `"Resource": "*"` means everything on everything, which breaks least privilege.
Pretty printing
`json.dumps(data, indent=2)` prints JSON with line breaks and indents, which makes a messy API response readable in seconds.

play.p: The policy is a JSON string. Run it, then change the second statement's Action to `s3:ListBucket`.
play.code:
import json
policy = '{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"}, {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*"}]}'
doc = json.loads(policy)
for st in doc["Statement"]:
    print(st["Effect"], st["Action"], st["Resource"])

real: On the job
Cloud security reviews often start with "find every policy that allows `*`". A short script over exported IAM policies does it for hundreds of roles at once.
myth: JSON is a Python thing.
JSON is a language-neutral text format used everywhere on the web. Python just happens to map it neatly onto dictionaries and lists.

quiz.w: JSON numbers become Python ints, so you get 3, not text.
There are two statements in the list.

o: It allows every action on everything
quiz.w: It gives full admin rights, the opposite of least privilege.

challenge.p: Print `WARNING: wildcard action` for every statement whose Action is `"*"`.
challenge.hint: Loop over `doc["Statement"]` and check `st["Action"] == "*"`.

recap: `json.loads` turns JSON text into Python data.
Reach into nested data one key at a time.
IAM policies are JSON statements.
`"Action": "*"` breaks least privilege.

lessons.sub: Subnets and private ranges without mistakes.
learn: The ipaddress module
`ipaddress` understands IPv4 and IPv6. It can tell you if an address is private and whether it sits inside a network, so you don't parse dots by hand.

import ipaddress
ip = ipaddress.ip_address("10.10.10.20")
print(ip.is_private, ip in ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24"))
Networks
`ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24")` is a subnet. `ip in net` checks membership, and `net.num_addresses` tells you its size.

import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("10.10.10.0/24")
print(net.num_addresses, ipaddress.ip_address("10.10.10.20") in net)
Private isn't the same as safe
`is_private` also covers documentation ranges like 203.0.113.0/24. For "is this on the internet?", `is_global` is the stricter test.

play.p: Try different addresses and networks.
play.code:
import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/28")
for ip in ["192.168.1.5", "192.168.1.20", "8.8.8.8"]:
    a = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    print(ip, a in net, a.is_private)

real: On the job
A SIEM exports 300 alerts as JSON. A script loads them, keeps the ones whose source IP isn't private, and prints a short list of external addresses to check against threat intel.

tryit.p: Load a small list of alerts and print only the ones from public addresses. Note that documentation ranges like 203.0.113.0/24 also count as private; `is_global` is the stricter test.

myth: Working out subnets by hand is safer.
It's where mistakes creep in. The ipaddress module gets /27s and /29s right every time.

quiz.w: 8.8.8.8 is a public address, so it isn't private.

quiz.code:
import ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/26")
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.70") in net)
quiz.w: A /26 starting at .0 covers .0 to .63, so .70 is outside it.
A /28 has 2 to the power of 4 addresses, which is 16.

challenge.p: Print only the addresses that are inside `10.10.10.0/24`, one per line.
challenge.hint: Loop, convert each with `ipaddress.ip_address(ip)`, and test `in net`.

recap: `ip_address` and `ip_network` do the maths for you.
`ip in net` checks membership.
`num_addresses` gives a subnet's size.
`is_global` is stricter than `not is_private`.

lessons.sub: Filter and transform a list in one line.
learn: The pattern
`[x for x in items if condition]` builds a new list. It's the loop-plus-if from Lesson 5, written in one line.

ports = [21, 22, 80, 443]
print([p for p in ports if p < 100])
Transforming
The first part can change each item: `[ip.strip() for ip in lines]` cleans every line at once.
Keep them readable
If a comprehension needs two conditions and a nested loop, a normal for loop is clearer. Readable beats clever.

play.p: Change the condition, or transform each item, for example `p + 1`.
play.code:
ports = [21, 22, 23, 80, 443, 3389]
print([p for p in ports if p in (21, 23)])
print([f"port-{p}" for p in ports[:2]])

real: On the job
Turning 300 raw log lines into a clean list of external IPs is often one comprehension: `[ip for ip in ips if not ipaddress.ip_address(ip).is_private]`.

quiz.code: print([n for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] if n % 2 == 0])
quiz.w: Only the even numbers pass the condition.
Each item is changed with `.upper()`.

quiz.q: When is a normal for loop better than a comprehension?
quiz.w: Comprehensions are for simple filters and changes; complex logic reads better as a loop.

challenge.p: Use a comprehension to keep only the usernames that start with `adm`, then print the list.
challenge.hint: `[u for u in users if u.startswith("adm")]`
challenge.solution:
users = ["admin", "kane", "adm-backup", "guest"]
print([u for u in users if u.startswith("adm")])

recap: `[x for x in items if test]` filters.
The first part can transform each item.
Use comprehensions for simple jobs.
Readable beats clever.

lessons.sub: A classic cipher, and why it's easy to break.
learn: Shifting letters
A Caesar cipher shifts each letter a fixed number of places: with a shift of 3, A becomes D. It's a teaching cipher, not real security.
Letters as numbers
`ord("a")` is 97 and `chr(97)` is "a". Shift with `(ord(c) - 97 + k) % 26 + 97`; the `% 26` wraps z back round to a.
print(ord("a"), chr(100))
Why it's weak
There are only 25 possible shifts, so a loop can try them all in a blink. That's a brute-force attack on the key space.

play.p: Change the message or the shift. A shift of -3 decrypts.

real: On the job
Nobody uses Caesar ciphers for real, but CTF challenges and malware analysis often use simple shifts and XOR to hide strings. Spotting and reversing them is a useful skill.
myth: A secret algorithm keeps data safe.
Security should rest on the key, not on hiding the method (Kerckhoffs's principle). Caesar fails both ways: the method is known and the key space is tiny.

quiz.w: Shifting a by 3 gives d.
`% 26` wraps past z back to the start, so z shifted by 2 is b.

quiz.q: How many different keys does a Caesar cipher on a to z have?
quiz.w: A shift of 26 gets you back where you started, so only 25 shifts change anything.

challenge.p: Brute-force it: print the shift that turns `khoor` into `hello`.
challenge.hint: Loop `for k in range(26):` and print k when `caesar(secret, -k) == "hello"`.

recap: Caesar shifts letters by a fixed key.
`ord` and `chr` turn letters into numbers and back.
`% 26` wraps around the alphabet.
A tiny key space falls to brute force.

lessons.sub: Spreadsheet exports are everywhere in security.
learn: The csv module
`csv.DictReader` reads each row as a dictionary keyed by the header row, so you can write `row["user"]` instead of counting columns.
Files or text
On Kali you'd use `open("logins.csv", newline="")`. Here, `io.StringIO(data)` makes a string behave like a file, so you can practise in the app.
Why not split on commas
A field like `"Smith, Jane"` contains a comma. The csv module handles quotes correctly; `.split(",")` doesn't.

play.p: Print a different column, or filter on `result`.
play.code:
import csv, io
data = """time,user,result,src
09:01,kane,success,10.10.10.10
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:03,admin,fail,198.51.100.23"""
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):
    print(row["user"], row["result"])

real: On the job
Entra ID, Okta and most firewalls export sign-in logs as CSV. A short script that counts failures per user is often faster than building a SIEM query for a one-off question.
myth: CSV is just text, so `.split(",")` is enough.
Quoted fields can contain commas and line breaks. Use the csv module and avoid subtle bugs.

quiz.code:
import csv, io
data = "user,result\nkane,success\nroot,fail"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)))
print(rows[1]["user"])
quiz.w: DictReader skips the header and the second data row's user is root.
The csv module keeps the quoted name together.

quiz.q: What does `csv.DictReader` use as the keys?
quiz.w: Each row becomes a dictionary keyed by the header names.

challenge.p: Count the failed logins and print `3 failed`.
challenge.hint: Loop over the DictReader and add 1 when `row["result"] == "fail"`.
challenge.solution:
import csv, io
data = """time,user,result,src
09:01,kane,success,10.10.10.10
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:02,root,fail,203.0.113.7
09:03,admin,fail,198.51.100.23"""
fails = 0
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):
    if row["result"] == "fail":
        fails += 1
print(fails, "failed")

recap: `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary.
Use `newline=""` when opening CSV files.
Don't split on commas by hand.
Sign-in exports are often CSV.

lessons.sub: Bundle data and the code that uses it.
learn: What a class is
A class is a blueprint. `class Alert:` describes what every alert has (its data) and can do (its methods). Each alert you create is an object.
__init__ and self
`__init__` runs when you create an object and stores its data on `self`. `self.ip` is this alert's IP.
Methods
A method is a function inside the class that uses `self`. `a.is_high()` reads naturally and keeps the rule next to the data.

play.p: Create another alert with a different score and check it.

real: On the job
Security tools and SDKs, boto3 included, hand you objects with methods. Writing a small class yourself makes their documentation far easier to read.

quiz.w: `a.score` is the value stored by `__init__`.
3 is less than 7, so `is_high` returns False.

quiz.q: What does `self` refer to inside a method?
o: The object the method was called on
quiz.w: `a.is_high()` passes `a` in as `self`.

challenge.p: Add a method `label()` that returns `"HIGH"` when the score is 7 or more and `"LOW"` otherwise, then print `Alert("1.2.3.4", 9).label()`.
challenge.hint: Inside the class, add `def label(self):` and return "HIGH" if `self.score >= 7`.

recap: A class is a blueprint; objects are made from it.
`__init__` stores data on `self`.
Methods are functions that use `self`.
SDKs like boto3 are full of objects.

lessons.t: Why sockets and boto3 need a real machine
lessons.sub: Some code can't run in a browser, and shouldn't.
learn: The browser sandbox
Python here runs inside your browser, which can't open raw network connections, read your files or use your AWS keys. That's a safety feature.
A tiny port check
Loop over a few ports and report the open ones. This is a TCP connect check: the full handshake completes, unlike Nmap's SYN scan.

import socket
host = "10.10.10.20"
for port in [22, 135, 445, 3389]:
    s = socket.socket()
    s.settimeout(1)
    if s.connect_ex((host, port)) == 0:
        print(port, "open")
    s.close()
Always set a timeout
Without a timeout, a filtered port can hang your script for a long time. `s.settimeout(1)` gives up after a second. Close each socket when you're done with it.
What boto3 is

boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. On Kali, install it with `sudo apt install python3-boto3`, because plain pip is blocked outside a virtual environment. Cloud security teams use it to audit settings across many accounts and services.
Credentials
boto3 finds credentials from `aws configure`, environment variables or an IAM role. Never put access keys in your code. Use a read-only role for audits, following least privilege.
Command-line arguments
`argparse` turns `python3 tool.py ssh.log --threshold 5` into named values, with help text for free. It makes a script reusable without editing the code.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count failed logins")
p.add_argument("logfile")
p.add_argument("--threshold", type=int, default=5)
args = p.parse_args()
print(args.logfile, args.threshold)
real: On the job

Misconfigured cloud storage is behind many data exposures, and it's OWASP 2025 A02. A short boto3 script that flags buckets without a public access block is a classic cloud security interview project.
myth: Writing your own scanner makes you stealthier than Nmap.
A connect scan completes the handshake, so it's noisier than a SYN scan and easily logged. Use Python for automation, not stealth.

tryit.p: Save the learn card's code as portcheck.py and run it. Then compare the result with `sudo nmap -sS -p 22,135,445,3389 10.10.10.20`.

quiz.q: What does `connect_ex` return when a port is open?
quiz.w: It returns an error number, and 0 means no error: the connection succeeded.

o: So filtered ports don't hang the script
quiz.w: A firewall that silently drops packets never answers. The timeout stops your script waiting.

quiz.q: Where should a boto3 script get its AWS credentials?
o: From aws configure, environment variables or an IAM role
Hard-coded at the top of the script
From a comment in the code
quiz.w: Hard-coded keys leak through repos and screenshots. Let boto3 find credentials outside the code.

quiz.q: Why give an audit script a read-only role?
o: If the script or key leaks, it can't change anything
quiz.w: Least privilege limits the damage from a compromised script or credential.

quiz.q: You open report.txt with mode "w". What happens to what was already in it?
o: New text is added to the end
quiz.w: "w" truncates the file. Use "a" to append instead.

challenge.p: Without running it: what should a boto3 audit script use for credentials, and which permissions should its role have?
challenge.hint: Think about where secrets should never live, and about least privilege.
challenge.solution: Credentials from an IAM role or `aws configure` (never hard-coded in the script), and a read-only role with only the permissions the audit needs.

recap: Browsers can't open sockets or read your AWS keys.
Always set a socket timeout.
boto3 gets credentials from the environment or a role, never the script.
Audit with read-only roles, in accounts you own.

lessons.sub: Put the whole track together in one tool.
learn: The goal
Read an SSH log, find failed logins, count them per source IP and print the IPs over a threshold. It uses files, regex, Counter, functions, error handling and argparse.
The plan
Break it into steps before writing code: get arguments, open the file safely, match each line, count, then report. Each step is a few lines you already know.
Practise here, then build it on Kali
Write the core here against the sample log. Then add argparse and file reading on Kali, as in the Try it card.

play.p: This is the core of the detector. Change the threshold and run it.
play.code:
import re
from collections import Counter
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
pattern = re.compile(r"Failed password .* from (\S+)")
counts = Counter()
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    m = pattern.search(line)
    if m:
        counts[m.group(1)] += 1
for ip, n in counts.most_common():
    if n >= 2:
        print(f"{ip} {n} failures")

real: On the job
Interviewers love a small, working tool you can explain line by line. “I wrote a script that finds brute-force sources in SSH logs” shows Python, log analysis and security thinking at once.
myth: Portfolio projects have to be big to count.
A small tool with a clear README, sample output and an honest list of limitations beats an unfinished large one.

tryit.p: Start SSH, fail a few logins with `ssh nobody@localhost`, then run `sudo journalctl -u ssh > ssh.log` and `python3 bruteforce.py ssh.log --threshold 2`. Stop SSH afterwards.

quiz.q: Which part of the detector pulls the source IP out of each line?
quiz.w: `(\S+)` after "from " captures the IP, and `.group(1)` returns it.

quiz.q: Why compile the regex once with `re.compile` outside the loop?
o: It avoids re-processing the pattern on every line
quiz.w: Python caches patterns anyway, but compiling once is clearer and avoids repeated work on huge logs.

quiz.q: Which extension would best catch a successful brute-force attack?
o: Flag an IP with many failures followed by a success
quiz.w: Many failures then a success from the same source is a classic sign that a password was guessed.

challenge.p: Extend the detector: also print `ALERT` before any IP with 3 or more failures, like `ALERT 203.0.113.7 3`.
challenge.start:
import re
from collections import Counter
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
pattern = re.compile(r"Failed password .* from (\S+)")
counts = Counter()
for line in LOG.splitlines():
    m = pattern.search(line)
    if m:
        counts[m.group(1)] += 1
challenge.hint: Loop over `counts.items()` and print when `n >= 3`.
challenge.solution:
import re
from collections import Counter
LOG = """Nov 17 09:14:01 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50122 ssh2
Nov 17 09:14:05 kali sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50124 ssh2
Nov 17 09:15:12 kali sshd[815]: Accepted publickey for kane from 10.10.10.10 port 51000 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:40 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40001 ssh2
Nov 17 09:16:44 kali sshd[818]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 50130 ssh2"""
pattern = re.compile(r"Failed password .* from (\S+)")
counts = Counter()
for line in LOG.splitlines():
